title: DSC — Discite Computatrum Scientia
subtitle: Computer science education that doesn't need a computer.

sections.heading: The Why
sections.content: There are millions of kids in South Africa and across the developing world who will never touch a computer in a classroom. But computational thinking — decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithms — doesn't need a screen. It needs a teacher who knows how to play the right games. DSC is a curriculum of unplugged activities: board games, card games, group challenges, storytelling, and physical movement. No computers required, every concept sticks.

sections.heading: The Vision
sections.content: Years ago I wrote that every child should learn computer science, not to become a programmer, but to become a creator — someone who understands the logic behind the tools they use, rather than just consuming whatever tech hands them. That philosophy hasn't aged a day. DSC is the practical manifestation of that idea: a full lesson plan series for Grades R through 1, built for the reality of South African classrooms where a teacher's creativity matters more than a computer lab budget.

sections.heading: What's Coming
sections.content: lesson plans that a teacher can pick up and run with in 30 minutes, no training needed
items: A Magic Forest board game that teaches sequencing and conditionals through storytelling
Complete Grade 1 and Grade R term plans mapped to the SA CAPS curriculum
Teacher training materials — because the best unplugged lesson falls flat if the facilitator isn't confident
Assessment frameworks that measure computational thinking without a written test
A community contribution model so other educators can adapt and share their own lessons

sections.heading: Stay Tuned
sections.content: I'm rebuilding, updating, and expanding this project from the ground up. Six years of new ideas, deeper understanding of how kids learn, and — honestly — a much better sense of what actually works in a real classroom. The early materials were promising. The next iteration is going to be something I'm genuinely proud to put my name on.
